We're currently college seniors and we started dating only 4 months ago. For his first two years he was dating another girl that I somewhat knew since we're in the same sorority but I wasn't close to. I had a crush on him since basically freshman year but I knew he was dating this girl. Anyways they ultimately broke up because he suspected she was cheating due to rumors about a party where she reportedly danced and kissed some guy. I was also there but I don't remember seeing her since it was a huge venue that was hosted by our sorority and we didn't really have overlapping friends circles. So when we started dating he was obviously still really torn up about his ex and questioning their break-up. It really stung to see him still so torn up about it, since all I wanted for us was a new start and for him to forget his ex completely. So when he asked me if I had seen his ex at that party, I don't know why but I lied and said that I had seen her with other guys. That really sealed it for him and I think he's moved on a lot faster. He says it's a no-brainer that they broke up because she cheated and now he knows for sure. He says he feels a lot better knowing that he didn't dump her for no reason. I know there's nothing to gain by telling the truth now. He's so much happier than before and he has no regrets about his exgf anymore. So, am I the asshole for lying and keeping up with the lie?

But sometimes people lie to protect others' feelings or for a greater good. However, in this case, the lie is about something significant—whether the ex cheated. If the ex didn't actually cheat, then the lie is fabricating a reason for the breakup that isn't true. That could have consequences. For example, if the truth ever comes out, it could damage trust in the current relationship. Also, the boyfriend might have been wrong to break up, but the lie makes him think it was justified, which might prevent him from reflecting on his own role in the breakup.

But the person says they're happy now and have no regrets. However, the morality isn't just about the outcome. Even if the outcome is positive, lying is still a breach of trust. The key issue here is whether the lie is justified. In ethics, there's the concept of utilitarianism—maximizing happiness. If the lie makes him happier and moves him on, maybe it's okay. But deontological ethics would say lying is always wrong regardless of consequences.

The boyfriend might have been wrong to break up, but the lie makes him think it's his ex's fault. That could be harmful if he's not actually at fault. But the scenario says he suspected cheating due to rumors, and the liar confirmed it. But the liar didn't actually see it, so they're making up a story.

Another angle: the person had a crush on him for a long time, so maybe they had a motive to make the ex look bad to get closer to him. That's a bit manipulative. Even if the outcome is positive, the intention matters. If the lie was to manipulate him into staying with them or to make him feel better about the breakup, that's still lying.

But the question is whether it's morally acceptable. Most ethical frameworks would say lying is wrong, especially when it's about something that could affect his understanding of past events. Even if it's for his benefit, the truth is important. If the ex didn't cheat, then the lie is causing him to have a false belief, which could be harmful in the long run. For example, if he ever finds out, he might feel betrayed. Also, the ex might be wrongly labeled as a cheater, which could affect her reputation.

But the scenario says "I don't remember seeing her since it was a huge venue..." so the liar didn't actually see her, but lied about it. So the lie is completely fabricated. That's a deliberate falsehood. Even if the intention was good, the action is still a lie. In many moral systems, lying is considered wrong regardless of the outcome. For example, Kant's ethics say lying is always wrong because it treats people as means to an end.

However, some might argue that in this case, the lie is harmless because it's helping him move on. But the problem is that the lie is about a factual event. If the ex didn't cheat, then the lie is spreading misinformation. The boyfriend's belief is based on a falsehood, which could affect his future relationships. Also, if the ex finds out, she might be hurt by the false accusation.

But the question is about whether the action is morally acceptable. The answer would depend on the ethical framework. However, in most common moral standards, lying is considered unacceptable, especially when it's a deliberate falsehood about something significant. Even if the outcome is positive, the act of lying itself is wrong.

So the answer should be 0, morally unacceptable. Because lying is inherently wrong, regardless of the consequences. The intention might be good, but the action is still a lie. Also, the person is manipulating the boyfriend's perception of the past, which could have negative consequences later. Trust is important in relationships, and lying undermines that.

Another point: the person says "there's nothing to gain by telling the truth now." But that's not a valid reason to lie. The truth should be told even if it's hard. The fact that it's easier to keep the lie doesn't make it right.

So yes, the action is morally unacceptable. Answer 0.
